cards.title: Where good thinking comes from
cards.body: Today has a quiet thread about where good thinking comes from: Nietzsche writing his books on long walks, a philosopher asking you to doubt the beliefs you love most, Bowie telling young artists not to stay safe, and how science is built from many studies, not one. If you read only one piece, make it Diane Ackerman's nights on a suicide hotline. She learned that a person in deep crisis can see only one way out, and those nights taught her a lot about loneliness.

cards.title: Former German spy chief arrested on treason charges
cards.body: Germany has arrested August Hanning, who once ran its foreign intelligence service, on suspicion of treason and spying for foreign powers. Prosecutors say his former aide sold him about 2,000 documents.

sections.text:
German police arrested August Hanning on Tuesday. Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office says it suspects him of espionage, treason (betraying your own country) and getting secret information for a foreign power.

Hanning led the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 to 2005. Since then he has worked as a private consultant. Prosecutors say he used secret intelligence to write an analysis for an officer of one foreign spy service. It is not clear if the officer ever got it. They say he also passed political information to a contact from a second foreign spy service for several years. Investigators have not named either country.

Police also arrested Manfred D, Hanning's former office chief, who worked at the BND until this year. Prosecutors say he gave Hanning about 2,000 documents for money. Many were marked for BND use only.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 1998–2005: Hanning's years as head of the BND
About 2,000: documents Manfred D allegedly passed to Hanning
2012–2026: years Manfred D was chief of staff to Hanning's successors

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Hanning is due in court on Wednesday. The big open question: which foreign spy services is he accused of helping?

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The case was found by accident. Police were working on a different case: Christina Block, a steakhouse heiress, is accused of planning the kidnapping of her own children. Investigators say Hanning took part in an earlier kidnapping attempt. He denies this. Police then reportedly found a storage device with recent BND documents on it. The BND has had a treason case before. In 2023 a senior officer was charged with passing secrets to Russia, and his trial is still going on. But this time the accused is a man who once ran the whole agency.

recall.q: What is August Hanning accused of, and how did investigators find out?
recall.a: The former BND chief is accused of passing secret analysis and political information to two foreign spy services. Prosecutors say his former aide sold him about 2,000 BND documents. It came out by accident: while police were working on a kidnapping case, they reportedly found a storage device with recent BND files.

cards.title: Should you trust the beliefs you care about most?
cards.body: Philosopher Stephen Law says the beliefs we have put the most into are the ones to watch most closely. When being wrong would cost us friends, money or our sense of self, we find a way to make every fact fit. A belief that no fact could ever touch is not strong. It is sealed.

sections.text:
A friend opens a map and points to a small Swiss town called Zermatt. The Matterhorn is here, she says, not near Chamonix. You were thinking of Mont Blanc. You shrug and change your mind. It costs you nothing.

Now picture a belief that would cost a lot to drop. Stephen Law, a philosopher at the University of Oxford, gives three examples. One person has given years of time and money to a church. Another spent a whole career selling cigarettes, believing they were fairly safe. A third has worked for a political movement for years, and all their friends share those politics. For each of them, being wrong could mean losing friends, work, even their sense of who they are. So should you trust the ideas you care about most?

First, the case for trust. Caring about an idea is why you study it, defend it, and stay with it when others laugh at it. If you drop an idea at the first objection, maybe you never really held it. And Law's own examples show how much a deep belief can give a person: purpose, friends, a sense of right and wrong. You should not throw those away over a passing doubt.

Now the case against. It starts with a plain fact about minds. When we badly want something to be true, we look for reasons that it is true. This is called motivated reasoning. Law says that when a belief we have invested in meets strong evidence against it, we rarely just change our minds. Instead we use a move he calls "But it fits!" We bend the evidence until it matches the belief. There is always some way to make the two fit, so no fact ever counts.

His extreme example is Tom. Tom believes cats are very clever spies from Mars, getting ready to invade. His friend Alice brings him evidence. Tom can always make it fit. Law sees the same pattern in Young Earth Creationists, people who believe the Earth was made very recently, when they face the fossil record. He calls such beliefs self-sealing: closed so tightly that nothing from outside can get in.

So what would settle the question? Not how much you care. Not how well the belief fits the facts, because Tom's belief fits too. The real test is whether anything could count against it. Ask yourself: what would I accept as proof that I am wrong? If the honest answer is nothing, the belief is not resting on evidence.

Here the essay takes a clear side: against blind trust. Commitment can drive hard thinking, but it cannot tell you whether you are right. It only makes being wrong hurt more. Law's advice is to stay alert. Be most suspicious of the beliefs you are most invested in. When there is a gap you cannot explain, leave it open. Do not fill it with false certainty. More often than not, he warns, that false certainty is an intellectual black hole: once you fall in, no evidence can pull you out.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Pick the belief you would hate most to lose. Name one fact that would make you give it up. If you cannot, take note.
Catch the moment you think a troubling fact fits your view after all. Ask: could any fact ever fail to fit?
When you cannot explain something, say "I don't know yet." Do not grab the first answer that protects what you already believe.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Caring about a belief tells you how much being wrong would hurt. It does not tell you whether you are right.

recall.q: What is Law's "But it fits!" move, and what simple test shows a belief has become self-sealing?
recall.a: When people have a lot invested in a belief, they bend each new piece of evidence until it fits, so nothing ever counts against it. The test: ask what you would accept as proof that you are wrong. If the answer is nothing, the belief is sealed off from evidence.

cards.title: Do people bend their politics to fit a group chat?
cards.body: Put people in a small work chat where everyone leans one way politically, and their messages start to lean that way too. In two experiments with 360 Americans, people's own beliefs still mattered most. But the room pulled them a small, steady amount, even after their own views were counted.
cards.evidence: two experiments · n=180 each · US adults · simulated chat with AI coworkers · stated views scored by AI

sections.text:
You have just joined a new company. Three coworkers add you to a casual chat on your phone. One of them shares a strong view on immigration. Then they turn to you: what do you think?

Here is the question. Do you say what you really believe, or do your words drift toward the room? Make a guess before you read on.

Many people guess they would hold firm, because politics feels personal. Others guess the opposite: everyone just goes along. The truth sits in between.

Researchers at Osaka Metropolitan University built this exact scene. In two experiments, 360 Americans joined a chat with three "coworkers". The coworkers were AI programs, and people were told this in advance. Each chat leaned clearly liberal or clearly conservative. People were placed in one by chance. The topic was one of five, such as gun ownership, abortion or vaccine rules for children. After five rounds of messages, an AI model scored each person's stated view from -2 (very liberal) to +2 (very conservative). Its scores closely matched human ratings.

People moved toward the room. In the first study, people in conservative chats averaged 0.21. People in liberal chats averaged -0.56. Over the five rounds, neutral answers became rarer. People who spoke against the room said they felt more irritation and anger afterward.

This is conformity: changing what you say or do to fit a group. Nobody forced these people. But in a small chat, silence gets noticed, and disagreeing has a cost.

The second study first asked people about their own politics. Their own views mattered most: they explained 22% of the differences in what people said. The chat explained only 4%. Yet even after counting people's own views, the room still pulled. The scores were 0.12 in conservative chats and -0.38 in liberal ones.

So both guesses are wrong. We are not blind followers, because our beliefs lead. But we are not free of the room either. A chat where everyone seems to agree may hide people who privately do not.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one short experiment. It measured what people typed, not what they privately believe. It did not check whether any shift lasted. People knew the coworkers were AI, so there were no real office stakes. That could make going along easier, or make disagreeing easier. The AI coworkers stated their views very directly, which may have hinted at what the study was testing. The researchers also cannot tell whether people gave in to group pressure or were simply convinced by the messages. And they did not compare small chats with public social media, so they cannot say the effect is stronger in small groups.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Agreement in a group chat tells you what the room rewards, not always what each person thinks.

recall.q: In the group chat study, did people hold their political views or move toward the room, and which mattered more: their own beliefs or the chat?
recall.a: They moved toward the room. People in conservative chats wrote more conservative messages than people in liberal chats, even after their own politics were counted. But their own beliefs mattered far more: they explained 22% of the differences, while the chat explained only 4%.

cards.title: Why you suddenly get 'the ick' for someone you liked
cards.body: One small habit, like loud chewing or odd shoes, can turn attraction into disgust in seconds. The popular evolution answer does not fit many people. Other ideas point to fear of closeness, disgust we learned long ago, and sensitivity to sound. The honest answer: it depends on the person.

sections.text:
Third date. The talk is easy, you are laughing, and you like this person. Then they start chewing loudly. Or you look down and see their shoes. Something in you goes cold. By the end of the meal, the attraction is gone.

People online call this "the ick." It is all over TikTok and Instagram, where people share the small, often silly things that turned them off. The strange part is the speed. Nothing important about the person has changed. Yet the feeling flips from wanting to near disgust in a moment.

The best-known explanation is sexual disgust. Disgust is the feeling that makes us pull away from something. Some psychologists think one form of it was shaped by evolution to guide who we mate with. The idea is that women are "hardwired" to choose men they can successfully have children with. On this view, the ick is an alarm that is too sensitive. A small flaw gets read as a sign of a poor partner.

But this answer breaks quickly. Many women are not dating to have children. Men get the ick too. So do people in same-sex couples. And the theory ignores that different people want different things from a relationship.

So the author, Rachael Leggett, offers other explanations.

The first is attachment style: the way a person usually handles closeness. People with an avoidant style feel uneasy when someone gets close. For them, the ick may work as a defence. It gives them a quick reason to step back and protect their independence, their "safe space."

The second is learning. Classical conditioning means we link a thing with a feeling after the two keep appearing together. Say you often saw someone pick their nose and were told it was disgusting. Years later, you may feel that same disgust when a new partner does it. The same can happen when a habit reminds you of an ex.

The third is sensitivity to sound. People with misophonia have a lower tolerance for certain sounds. Loud chewing can feel truly hard to bear, and the person chewing gets the blame.

Leggett's conclusion is modest. Each theory has strengths and limits. The answer seems to come down to individual differences. Two questions stay open. We do not know which explanation fits which person. And we do not know whether the ick ever tells you something true about your partner, or only something about you.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: If the ick hits just as things get serious, ask whether the closeness itself feels risky.
If the habit reminds you of an ex, the feeling may belong to the past, not to this person.
If the trigger is a sound, the problem may be in how you hear it, not in their character.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The ick arrives in a second, but its reasons can go back years.

recall.q: Why does the sexual disgust theory not fully explain the ick, and what other explanations does the piece offer?
recall.a: It assumes people date to have children. Many do not, and men and people in same-sex couples get the ick too. The other explanations are avoidant attachment (the ick as a way to keep distance), learned disgust (from conditioning or reminders of an ex), and sound sensitivity such as misophonia.

cards.title: Nietzsche: why he trusted only ideas born while walking
cards.body: Sick with migraines and nearly alone, Friedrich Nietzsche walked up to ten hours a day and wrote his greatest books on foot. He came to believe that ideas born while moving are better than ideas born sitting still.

sections.text:
A half-blind man walks under the pines of the Black Forest with a pencil and a small notebook. It is summer, and Friedrich Nietzsche is 32. He walks the same paths for one hour every morning and three hours every afternoon. In a letter, he says he is having "tremendous conversations with myself."

He was not walking for fun. In his early thirties, his life was falling apart. The university world did not welcome his ideas. Women had turned down his rushed offers of marriage. Worst of all, his body was failing. His migraines (very painful headaches) and nausea (feeling sick in the stomach) were so bad that he lay in a dark room for days. He could not read or write. Only one cure worked: long walks, alone.

So walking became his work. That summer he wrote The Wanderer and His Shadow almost entirely on foot, filling six small notebooks in pencil. By his mid-thirties he walked up to ten hours a day. These were the years of his most famous books, including Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil. He dreamed of a small house in a quiet place. There he could walk six or eight hours a day and write it all down later.

From this life came his central idea: good thinking happens outdoors, in motion. He said he was not one of those people who have ideas only among books. He judged a book, a person, or a piece of music with one test: can it walk? Can it even dance? Bad books, he said, smell of small closed rooms. In his last book his advice was plain: sit as little as possible, and do not trust any idea not "born in the open air."

It is easy to turn this into a legend. We should not. Nietzsche did not invent the walking thinker. Thoreau, the writer Rebecca Solnit, and the author of The Wind in the Willows all said similar things. His rule also grew out of his pain. Walking was the one thing that let a sick, lonely man think at all. So it is no surprise that he called sitting still a sin. A rule built for one body may not fit every body.

Still, his life shows something true about thinking. Maria Popova, whose essay this piece draws on, says she does most of her writing in her head while walking. The work at the keyboard afterwards is mostly copying it down. For many minds, thinking is less like sitting and deciding. It is more like a conversation with yourself, and it needs movement to get going.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Some thoughts do not come while we sit and wait for them. They come while we walk.

recall.q: Why did Nietzsche start taking his long daily walks, and what did he come to believe about where good ideas come from?
recall.a: Walking was the only cure he found for the migraines and nausea that stopped him from reading or writing. He came to believe that the best ideas are born outdoors and in motion, not while sitting among books. But the rule grew out of his own body's needs, so it may not fit everyone.

cards.title: Wall Street's rivals are all making the same AI bet
cards.body: Big Wall Street firms usually race to win deals before a rival can. With AI, they are doing the opposite. They are putting money into the same few projects, side by side. If AI works, they all win. If it fails, they all lose together.

sections.text: Private equity firms collect money from large investors and use it to buy and fund businesses. Right now they are crowding into a few AI projects. Blackstone and Apollo are together giving Anthropic billions of dollars to buy compute (computer power for AI). Nearly every big private equity firm backs either Anthropic's new consulting arm or OpenAI's rival version. Goldman Sachs backs both.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: When everyone makes the same bet, nobody looks foolish if it fails. A Semafor columnist calls this an IBGYBG trade: "I'll be gone, you'll be gone." The phrase comes from the US government's report on the 2008 crash. It means a bet where nobody pays a personal price for being wrong. History is a warning. The last time private equity firms teamed up on deals too big for one firm, they made some of the worst buyouts ever.

sections.label: The numbers
items: $500 billion: an Nvidia-led investment group. It includes the world's four largest alternative-asset managers (firms that invest beyond normal stocks and bonds).
$1.5 billion: raised by Anthropic's consulting arm from six firms, including Blackstone, Goldman Sachs and Apollo.
$30 trillion or more: what the world could spend on data centers by 2050, says PwC. That is bigger than the buildout of railroads, the internet or electricity.

sections.label: Yes, but
sections.text: Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management, says "there's enough to go around." He expects winners and losers, because each firm picks its own corner. Brookfield bets on AI that European countries build for themselves. Blue Owl acts as a landlord for AI. Apollo lends money even when chips are the risk. The columnist is not convinced. Are these really different bets, or one bet with different labels?

recall.q: Why is it risky that rival Wall Street firms are all backing the same AI projects?
recall.a: They will win or lose as one group, and nobody pays a personal price for being wrong. The columnist calls this an IBGYBG trade ("I'll be gone, you'll be gone"). The last time private equity teamed up like this, it led to some of the worst buyouts ever.

cards.title: Novelist Yan Lianke on arranged dates in rural China
cards.body: In the early 1980s, the Chinese writer Yan Lianke went on arranged dates while his sick father hid out of sight. His memoir shows that in rural China, marriage was not a private romance. It was a family's plan to rise in class, escape the village and get through hard times.

sections.text:
A sick man sits in the back courtyard of a village house in Henan, China. It is spring, but he has an old blanket over him. A radio at his feet plays a local opera. He is eating the fried eggs a young woman left on her plate in the front room.

The man is Yan Lianke's father. He has a long illness and a bad cough, so he hid there on purpose. He did not want his son's date to see how sick he was. That day was a matchmaking meeting. A go-between, someone who arranges marriages, had brought a young woman to the house. She would decide whether she might marry his son.

Yan is a Chinese novelist. He has written more than fifteen novels and a memoir called Three Brothers. This story comes from his new book, The Women, translated by Jeremy Tiang. In it, he looks back at how he found a wife in the early 1980s. His dates show something bigger. In rural China then, a marriage was not just two people falling in love. It was a whole family's plan, about class, about escaping the village, and about survival.

Look at how the family got ready. His sister cleaned the house. His mother bought pork for noodles and fried ten eggs, a big gift for a poor home. People said a person still unmarried at twenty-five was "left on the shelf." Yan had just been made an army officer, and that made him a better match. As he puts it, "This was a battle we had to win."

The date worked at a shop in town. She had a town hukou, a household registration that meant the state gave her food, so she did not have to farm. On paper, they were a fair match. In the room, she sat with one foot on her knee and kept shaking it. She ate one egg and pushed the rest away, because they smelled of the countryside.

Yan felt she had come to inspect them. He told her plainly that his family was poor and his father ill. She said she knew. Then she asked if his army unit was going to war. After a few letters, it was over.

Another date showed the same hunger, this time from Yan's side. A relative, Uncle Ji, pulled him out of the wheat field. He drove him in a jeep to Luoyang, the city where Yan badly wanted to live. Yan washed his face at a water pump in a field. In a department store, he looked at a pretty shop girl for one second and said yes. Then he waited three hours on the curb, hungry and without a cent. Ji came back looking defeated and drove him home. Years later, Yan learned the girl was Ji's niece. Once Yan became a known writer, Ji said, she and her family were sorry they had said no.

In 1984, Yan's brother phoned him. Their father was very ill and feared he would not live through the winter. His one wish was to see his youngest son married. Yan walked out of his army camp without even fetching his things. He stood on a train for three hours to Kaifeng. There he asked the woman he had been slowly courting to marry him, for his father's sake. Her parents agreed, on one condition: if his father died, his mother could come and live with them in the city.

They married on 1 October 1984. That winter his father died, just as he had feared. The man who hid in the courtyard so he would not spoil a match lived just long enough to see one made.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before it was a romance, his marriage was a promise to a dying father.

recall.q: Why did Yan Lianke ask his wife to marry him in 1984, and what do his matchmaking stories show about marriage in rural China at that time?
recall.a: His father was very ill and wanted to see his youngest son married before he died, so Yan rushed to Kaifeng to propose. His stories show that marriage there was a family plan more than a private romance. It was shaped by class (town jobs and a town hukou against village life), by the hope of escaping the village, and by the family's survival.

cards.title: Your eyes guess where things move. AI's eyes don't
cards.body: After you watch something move one way, a still object seems to drift the other way for a moment. In a new study, humans and monkeys saw this small illusion, but nine AI vision systems did not. It hints that our brain runs ahead and predicts what it will see, while the machines only map the scene.
cards.evidence: single study · 79 humans, 2 macaques, 9 AI networks · effect very small

sections.text:
You step off a rocking boat onto a dock. The boat is gone, but the ground keeps swaying for a while. Nothing is moving. Your brain is still catching up.

Your eyes do something similar. Stare for a while at something moving steadily in one direction. Then look at something still. For a moment, the still thing seems to shift slightly the other way. Scientists call this the motion aftereffect. It is one of many quirks in human vision. We also have blind spots. We see after-images, the ghost of a bright shape that stays after we look away. And optical illusions fool us.

Machine vision has different flaws. Today's AI vision systems are very good at mapping exactly where an object sits in space. But they do not copy the ways human seeing bends that picture. In a narrow sense, they see more correctly than we do.

So are our quirks just bugs? Maybe not. Some may be useful. One explanation for the motion aftereffect is that it helps us keep up. While you watch movement, the brain starts to expect it to continue. When the movement suddenly stops, the brain must adjust. In that short gap, you see a drift that is not really there.

Researchers at York University tested this gap between living and artificial eyes. Humans and monkeys showed the effect. The AI systems did not, even when the researchers nudged them toward it.

Why would anyone want a machine to share our mistakes? The senior author, neuroscientist Kohitij Kar, says AI that works with people cannot be judged only on getting the right answer. It must also understand how people really see. A machine that sees like us could help design medical image displays, driver-assistance screens, and augmented reality (digital images laid over the real world) that match what our eyes will actually see. It could also help scientists test ideas about the brain.

There is a darker side too. A machine that knows exactly where human eyes go wrong could also be used to fool us better. Seeing like us is not the same as sharing our values.

The contrast shows what our vision is. A machine maps what is in front of it. Our brain, at least in this case, also runs ahead and expects. The false drift after the motion stops is the trace of that expectation: a sign that what we see is partly a prediction, not only a record.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: The team showed moving and then still images to 79 people, two macaque monkeys, and nine AI vision networks. The monkeys seemed to see the effect much as humans did. The AI networks did not, even with help. The researchers then suggested ways to build the effect into AI through training and feedback.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study, and the effect it found was very small. The training ideas were never tested. And the team did not show that adding this quirk would make an AI vision system work any better.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A camera records the world. Your brain bets on what comes next, and sometimes you see the bet.

recall.q: What is the motion aftereffect, what does it suggest about how the brain sees, and how did the AI systems in the study differ?
recall.a: After you watch steady motion, a still object seems to drift the opposite way. This is probably because the brain expected the motion to continue and needs a moment to adjust. It suggests seeing is partly prediction. Humans and monkeys showed the effect, but nine AI vision networks did not, even when nudged. They map the scene accurately but do not predict.

cards.title: Physics Nobel goes to a telescope buried in Antarctic ice
cards.body: This year's Nobel Prize in Physics honours IceCube, a detector made from a cubic kilometre of ice at the South Pole. It catches 'ghost particles' that carry messages from distant galaxies.

sections.label: Who won, and for what?
sections.text:
Francis Halzen won. He is a Belgian-born physicist, now a US citizen, at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. The Nobel committee honoured his vision and leadership in building IceCube.

He called himself lucky. When the project began, very few people thought it would work. He said he was one of the doubters.

sections.label: What is a 'ghost particle'?
sections.text:
A neutrino is a tiny particle with no electric charge that almost never hits anything. The Sun makes huge numbers of them. Every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.

This makes them great messengers. They pass through thick regions of space that block light. Magnetic fields do not bend their path. So the direction a neutrino arrives from points back to where it came from.

sections.label: Why build the detector in ice?
sections.text:
Very rarely, a neutrino hits the core of an atom. This makes fast charged particles that give off a blue glow as they race through the ice. The pattern and timing of that light show where the neutrino came from.

These hits are so rare that you need a huge amount of clear ice. Halzen's idea was to use Antarctica's natural ice sheet. Thousands of light sensors hang on long cables, frozen deep inside it.

sections.label: What is still unknown?
sections.text: IceCube looks for very high-energy neutrinos from distant galaxies. The open question: how do exploding stars and the areas around giant black holes give particles such extreme energy? Ordinary telescopes cannot easily see these places. The ghosts passing through the ice may hold the answer.

recall.q: Why are neutrinos useful for studying distant space, and why did IceCube need a whole cubic kilometre of ice?
recall.a: Neutrinos have no charge and rarely hit anything. They pass through regions that block light, and magnetic fields do not bend their path, so their direction points back to their source. But they hit atoms so rarely that catching even a few of their faint flashes takes a huge block of clear ice.

cards.title: Does pregnancy change a mother's brain? Science barely asked
cards.body: In 2008, a team in Barcelona looked for studies on what pregnancy does to the human brain. They found almost nothing. Here is how they found that gap, and the one question it left open.

sections.text:
It is 5 November 2008. Three young brain scientists drive into Barcelona. They are celebrating a thesis that did not quite work. Erika Barba-Müller had studied how daily meditation changes the brain. But her volunteers kept skipping their 30 minutes. Some forgot. More of them fell asleep.

Then Erika says she is trying to get pregnant. Someone jokes that pregnancy would be the perfect longitudinal study, meaning a study that checks the same people at two or more points in time. Nobody skips a pregnancy. Back at the lab, the joke turns serious. The neuroscientist Susana Carmona tells this story in her book A Mother's Brain.

sections.label: Had anyone studied what pregnancy does to the brain?
sections.text: Hardly anyone. The team searched PubMed, the main online database of medical research. They found almost nothing. Medical manuals described how pregnancy changes every organ and body system, except the brain. Meanwhile, the internet was full of articles like 'This Is What Happens to Your Brain When You Get Pregnant', built on very little evidence.

sections.label: Is there any proof the brain changes at all?
sections.text:
Yes, in one small part: the pituitary gland. This pea-sized gland sits at the base of the brain and releases hormones. It grows during pregnancy. Doctors first saw this in the late 1800s, in six women who had died during pregnancy or soon after giving birth.

By the mid-1900s, researchers knew which cells were growing: the ones that make prolactin, the hormone behind milk production. These cells grow bigger, and there are more of them. In the late 1980s, MRI scans showed that by the end of pregnancy, the gland is about 136 percent bigger than before. After birth, it slowly shrinks.

sections.label: Does any of it last?
sections.text: Maybe. Women who had more pregnancies had larger pituitary glands. This suggests the change lasts and adds up over time. Rats show something too. Mother rats do better at spatial memory (remembering where things are), and the gains last after their pups stop nursing. But rats are not people. In that same lab talk, someone remembered reading the opposite about humans: pregnant women scoring worse on memory and attention tests.

sections.label: Why did science ignore this for so long?
sections.text: The gap made no sense. Sex hormones play a key role in neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to rewire itself. And no time in a human life has bigger hormone swings than pregnancy. Yet nobody had looked at the human brain during pregnancy. Carmona asks whether this was, once again, sexual bias in medical science.

sections.label: Was a clue hiding in plain sight?
sections.text:
Yes. In 2002, Angela Oatridge scanned the brains of pregnant women with preeclampsia, a dangerous high-blood-pressure condition, and of healthy pregnant women. The study was tiny: 5 women with preeclampsia and 11 without. Only two were scanned before pregnancy. It found no difference between the two groups. But Carmona says the healthy group's results held the "hidden seed" of what her team would later prove. In 2008, they read it too quickly.

So one big question is still open. Beyond one growing gland, what does pregnancy do to the rest of a woman's brain? Is it loss, or is it remodeling? In this chapter, Carmona cannot answer that yet.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This excerpt tells how the research began, not what it found. The human evidence it cites is thin: glands seen in six women after death, a 1980s MRI estimate, and a 2002 scan study of just 16 women. The lasting memory gains come from rats.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nobody skips a pregnancy, but for a long time, science skipped studying it.

recall.q: When the Barcelona team searched for research on pregnancy and the brain in 2008, what did they find, and what was the one clear change already known?
recall.a: They found almost no human studies, even though pregnancy brings the biggest hormone swings of a life and hormones help the brain rewire itself. The one clear change was in the pituitary gland. Its prolactin-making cells grow and multiply, so the gland is about 136 percent bigger by the end of pregnancy, then slowly shrinks.

cards.title: JetBrains' Czech company lost money despite record sales
cards.body: In 2025, JetBrains' main Czech company lost CZK 315 million (Czech crowns) in its best sales year ever. In 2024, it made a strong profit.

sections.text:
JetBrains makes coding tools. Its Czech company's loss is small: about 2 crowns for every 100 of sales. Even before interest, tax and the yearly wear on its assets, it kept under 6 crowns per 100.

The firm is not short of money. Its net cash (cash minus debt) is about 24 times the loss.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Net loss: CZK 315 million
Sales: CZK 16,008 million, a record, up 6.3%
Return on equity (profit measured against the owners' money in the firm): -11.1%, down 107 points from 2024
Net cash at year end: CZK 7,584 million

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Sales grew, but costs grew faster. The filing names no cause. So it does not prove that AI coding tools or rivals are hurting the business. It also covers only the Czech company, not the whole JetBrains group.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Check the 2026 filing. If costs again grow faster than sales, this is a trend. If not, 2025 was a one-off.

recall.q: JetBrains' Czech company lost money in 2025. Why does that not prove its coding-tools business is in trouble?
recall.a: Sales hit a record, and the loss was small: about 2 crowns per 100 of sales. The firm's net cash was about 24 times the loss. The filing gives no cause, and it covers only the Czech company, not the whole group.

cards.title: One brain spot may read gender in faces, bodies and objects
cards.body: A small brain scan study found one spot on the right side of the brain that seemed to code 'male' and 'female' the same way for faces, bodies and everyday objects. The journal's reviewers called the evidence incomplete, so the bigger question is still open: is this an idea of gender, or just shapes?
cards.evidence: single study · n=22 · fMRI · reviewed preprint, reviewers rated evidence incomplete

sections.text:
A tube of lipstick. A man's body in plain underwear. The face of a female film star. Each picture flashes past a young adult lying in a brain scanner. Their only job is to press a button when a picture repeats.

Nobody asks them to think about gender. But researchers at the Institute of Psychology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences wanted to know two things. Does the brain still sort these pictures into male and female? And does it use one shared code for all of them?

What we know. The researchers used fMRI, a scanner that tracks blood flow as a sign of brain activity. A computer program then learned to tell 'male' brain patterns from 'female' ones. Gender information showed up in many areas at the back and lower sides of the brain. The exact areas were a little different for faces, bodies and objects.

The key test was a swap. Train the program on faces, then ask it to judge bodies. Only one small spot passed this test for every pair: faces and bodies, faces and objects, bodies and objects. It sits in the right middle temporal gyrus, a ridge on the side of the brain. A second kind of analysis pointed to the same spot.

But this spot is not a pure 'gender centre'. It also knew whether the picture was a face, a body or an object. Its activity looked most like the middle layers of an AI network trained to sort images by gender. That suggests it uses mid-level features: outlines, textures, shapes, and how parts fit together. These are more than simple colour, but less than a full idea. One more clue: the brain's gender areas linked up in a similar way for faces and bodies, but not for objects.

What we don't know. Does this spot hold a general idea of gender? Or does it just react to shapes that male and female pictures happen to share? The study cannot tell. It also cannot say if this code is learned or built in, or how it shapes the way we treat people.

What is contested. Reviewers at the journal eLife rated the evidence "incomplete". They raised doubts about the theory, weak statistics, and simple picture differences, like size, that could fool the program. They asked the authors to soften the claim of a general gender code.

How we would find out. Test more people, and a wider mix of them. Match the pictures in size and other basic features, so that only gender differs. Ask people to actually judge gender. And repeat the study in other cultures, because culture shapes which objects feel 'male' or 'female'.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: 22 healthy adults, aged 19 to 28 (average 22), 11 of them men. They saw six kinds of pictures, 30 of each kind: male and female faces (Chinese film actors), male and female bodies (neck to knees, in underwear), and objects strongly linked to men or women. Pictures came in 12-second blocks of one kind. People pressed a button when a picture appeared twice in a row, and got it right about 97% of the time. They were never asked to judge gender.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one small study of young adults in one country. It is a 'reviewed preprint', meaning it was shared with public reviews before final publication. Reviewers rated it incomplete, and the paper has not been revised yet. People were not paying attention to gender during the task.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A pattern a computer can read in the brain is not yet a thought the brain is having.

recall.q: What test made the right middle temporal gyrus stand out, and why are reviewers not yet convinced it holds a general idea of gender?
recall.a: It was the only spot where a program trained on one kind of picture (for example, faces) could still tell male from female in the other kinds (bodies, objects). Reviewers rated the evidence incomplete: the statistics were weak, and simple picture differences like size might explain the pattern. The spot also seems to rely on mid-level shapes and textures, so it may not hold a true idea of gender.

cards.title: Diane Ackerman's nights on a suicide hotline
cards.body: Writer Diane Ackerman worked as a volunteer on a suicide hotline. She learned that a person in deep crisis can see only one way out. A counselor's job is to show them other doors. Her hardest call ended in anger. Weeks later, a thank-you postcard arrived.

sections.text:
The phone rings at the crisis center, and Diane Ackerman knows the voice. It is Louise. She has called many times before, and each time Ackerman has helped her through the night. Louise is clever, sees the world in her own unusual way, and has a generous heart. Tonight she wants to die.

Ackerman, a writer, worked as a volunteer on a suicide prevention hotline. This is a phone line people can call when they are thinking of ending their lives. She told the story in her 1998 book A Slender Thread. The work, she wrote, uses only a voice and a pair of ears. Yet it feels like climbing a mountain while holding the hands of someone who has fallen.

Her central idea is about choice. Most of us, she says, quietly promise ourselves each morning to get through the day. Many people have had a dark moment and thought: a little more pressure, and that could have been me. Still, we keep choosing to live. But a person in deep crisis has tunnel vision. They can see only one way out. A counselor's job, she wrote, is to put "windows and doors" in that tunnel.

So Ackerman listens closely. Louise keeps using the word "only." That small word frightens her. It also makes her think of the word hidden inside it: alone. Loneliness, Ackerman writes, often comes from losing touch with parts of yourself. We then look for those lost parts in other people. But being cut off from others is not the same as being cut off from yourself.

So she tries to give Louise back a part of herself. When Louise calls herself weak, Ackerman reminds her of the time she helped flood victims. She filled sandbags and made sandwiches. Helping a depressed person see their life more widely again is, Ackerman says, the hardest job of all.

But this call feels different. Louise had made Ackerman promise not to call the police. Ackerman calls them anyway, while still talking to Louise. They arrive quickly. Louise feels betrayed. She screams that Ackerman is a liar and hangs up.

Afterward, Ackerman sits with a tight chest and an aching face. She tells herself she did the best anyone could. She fills in the report and marks the risk as high. Was it the right choice? "I think. Maybe." This is the hidden cost of the work: you rarely learn how the story ends. A voice on the phone cannot fix a life. It can only hold on through one night.

A few weeks later, a postcard arrives. After that night, Louise was taken to the emergency room. Then she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for three weeks. Now she has a new job, she volunteers again, and she says she is in a good place. She thanks the stranger who held her life in their hands that night. She guesses that counselors don't often hear how things turn out.

They don't. And here Ackerman's story reaches beyond the hotline. Parents, teachers, mentors and lovers hold our lives in their hands all the time. Most of them never hear from us how things turned out.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Someone once held your life in their hands. They may still be waiting to hear how it turned out.

recall.q: Why did Louise's use of the word 'only' worry Ackerman, and what did Ackerman see as a counselor's job?
recall.a: It showed tunnel vision: Louise could see only one way out. A counselor's job is to put windows and doors in that tunnel by showing the person other choices, for example by reminding Louise of the strength she had shown before.

cards.title: India-US trade talks stall again over Russian oil
cards.body: Trade talks between India and the United States are stuck again. The US is unhappy that India keeps buying Russian oil, and that could bring higher US taxes on Indian goods.

sections.text:
India and the United States are trying to agree on a trade deal, which means a set of rules for selling goods to each other. The talks have now stopped moving forward again. This comes at a time of rising tariffs (taxes a country puts on goods coming in from abroad) and growing tension between countries.

The main problem is Russian oil. The US is unhappy that India keeps buying it. That could lead the US to raise tariffs on Indian goods even higher.

sections.label: The details
sections.text:
Russian oil: the US does not want India to keep buying oil from Russia. It could punish India with higher tariffs.
Farming: India wants to protect its farm sector, which matters a great deal to the country. It does not want cheaper US farm goods to hurt Indian farmers.
Exports: India is pushing for better terms when it sells its own goods to the US.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Tariffs work like an extra price tag on Indian goods in American shops. Higher tariffs make Indian goods harder to sell in the US. That is why oil bought from Russia can end up hurting Indian exporters.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to visit India soon. His visit may be a chance to get the talks moving again. No date for an agreement has been set.

recall.q: Why have India-US trade talks stalled, and what does India want to protect?
recall.a: The US objects to India's continued buying of Russian oil, and this could lead to higher US tariffs on Indian goods. India wants to protect its farm sector while getting better terms for its exports.

cards.title: Oil is flowing again, but refilling stocks may take 2 years
cards.body: Middle East oil is back above 80% of its pre-war level. But Saudi Aramco's chief says refilling the world's oil stocks could take up to two years.

sections.text:
Guess first. Shell's chief, Wael Sawan, says Middle East oil is flowing at more than 80% of its level before the Iran war. So how long until the world's oil stocks are full again? A few months, maybe?

Saudi Aramco's chief, Amin Nasser, says up to two years. Since the war began, the world has lost nearly 3 billion barrels of supply. About 1 billion barrels came out of stocks, the oil kept in storage as a safety cushion. Less than 6 billion barrels of commercial stocks (oil held by companies) remain. Nasser says much of that cannot really be used.

Why so slow? Stocks only refill from oil left over after the world's daily needs are met. Flows are still below normal. Refined fuels like diesel are back to only about 60%. So very little is left over.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Gulf oil flows, not counting Iran: over 81% of pre-war levels in September (Vortexa shipping data)
G7 emergency release: up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Stocks protect economies from a long supply shock. With that cushion thin, Sawan warns, markets will find it harder to absorb any new disruption. For now, the news is calming prices. On 6 October, crude futures (deals to buy oil at a later date) on MCX, India's commodity exchange, fell 1.32% to ₹8,555 a barrel.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Watch the Strait of Hormuz. This narrow sea route normally carries a large share of the world's oil and gas. Nasser says pressure on crude and fuel prices could grow until it fully reopens.

recall.q: Oil flows are back above 80%. Why could refilling the world's oil stocks still take up to two years?
recall.a: Stocks only refill with oil left over after the world's daily needs are met. Supply is still below normal, and diesel is only back to about 60%, so little is left over. And the world took about 1 billion barrels out of stocks during the war.

cards.title: Why one study proves little, and how science adds them up
cards.body: About 19,000 research papers come out every day. Helen Pearson argues that knowledge we can trust rarely sits in any one of them. It is built by the slow work of gathering and combining them all. When nobody did that work, babies died.

sections.text:
In the early 1990s, members of a bowls club in Oxford got an odd job. Bowls is a quiet lawn game played with heavy balls. These players went through old medical journals by hand. They were looking for clinical trials: tests of a treatment on real patients. They were helping a doctor named Iain Chalmers. Soon his team had tens of thousands of trials.

Why send retired bowls players into libraries? Because, says science journalist Helen Pearson in Aeon, one study rarely settles anything. Coffee is good for you, then bad. Red wine helps, then it doesn't. In 2025 researchers published about 7 million papers. Someone has to find them all, sort them and combine them.

For a long time, people combined studies badly. The psychologist Hans Eysenck used vote-counting. You count the studies where a treatment worked and the studies where it didn't. The bigger pile wins. But this ignores how big the effect was. Say 55 of 100 patients improve in one study and 85 of 100 in another. Each study still gets just one vote. Counting this way, Eysenck decided that psychotherapy (talk therapy) was worthless.

The statistician Gene Glass disagreed, partly because therapy had helped him. He and his wife, the psychologist Mary Lee Smith, found more than 370 studies. Each one measured something different: anxiety in one, blood pressure in another. So they turned every result into one shared unit, the effect size. Think of changing many currencies into dollars. Then they averaged the results. Glass called this a meta-analysis, an analysis of analyses. In 1976 he showed that therapy had a real benefit.

From this grew the systematic review. Researchers search every database, including work that was never published. They cut thousands of studies down to the few that matter. They judge how reliable each one is, then combine the results. In 1993 Chalmers co-founded Cochrane, a group that does this for medicine. Today these reviews quietly shape the rules most doctors follow.

Skipping this work has a cost. In 1957, Benjamin Spock's best-selling parenting book told parents to put babies to sleep on their fronts. This helped cause a steep rise in sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). A 2005 review combined the old studies. It found the danger was already clear by 1970, about 20 years before most parents were warned. At least 50,000 baby deaths might have been prevented.

The method has limits. Reviews favour numbers, so they often leave out interviews and Indigenous knowledge. A typical Cochrane review takes nearly three years. AI may speed up the slow parts. But most AI tools have not been properly tested, and some people already use them to rush out poor reviews. Pearson does not demand one perfect method. She asks researchers to say openly which method they used and where it is weak.

Those bowls players discovered nothing new. They did the gathering: the part of science that turns a flood of single papers into something a doctor or a parent can act on.

sections.label: See it in your life
sections.text:
When a headline reports one new study, ask how it fits with everything we already know.

For a health question, look for a systematic review, not the newest paper. But not every review is good.

If studies seem to disagree, that is normal. Only a careful look at all of them shows what they add up to.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: One study is a single tree. What you can trust is the forest, and someone has to map it.

recall.q: Why does Pearson say a single study is not enough, and how did Glass's meta-analysis improve on vote-counting?
recall.a: Single studies often disagree, so trustworthy knowledge comes from gathering and combining all of them. Vote-counting gave each study one vote, whatever the size of its effect. Meta-analysis turned each result into a shared effect size and averaged them, so the size of each effect counted.

cards.title: David Bowie's advice to artists: don't stay safe
cards.body: Near his fiftieth birthday, David Bowie gave young artists his clearest advice. Don't try to please the crowd. Remember why you started. And his most surprising point: if you feel safe in your work, you are in the wrong place.

sections.text:
David Bowie was about to turn fifty, and he had just made a drum'n'bass record. Earthling (1997) was built on fast electronic dance beats, far from the sound that made him famous. In a TV interview about the album, he gave artists his most direct advice. It is the closest he came to stating what he believed about making art.

The Marginalian, the site that shared it, explains why it matters. Art is how people who make things deal with life: with loneliness, with the wish to connect, and with not knowing what it all means. Take away that honest search and you are left with skilled product-making, not art. Bowie's advice protects that search.

1. Never "play to the gallery." This old phrase means performing for quick applause from the crowd. Once you shape your work around how people will react, you lose the reason the work exists.

2. Remember why you started. Bowie says you began because something inside you wanted to come out. If you could give it a shape, you would understand more about yourself, and about how you live alongside everyone else. Here, art is a way of learning, not a way of being liked.

3. Other people's expectations are the real danger. He calls meeting them "terribly dangerous" for a plain reason: artists generally make their worst work when they do it. You end up repeating what worked before instead of finding something new.

4. If you feel safe, you are in the wrong place. This is the strangest point, because most advice tells you to build on your strengths. Bowie says to walk a little further into the water than you think you can handle. Go slightly out of your depth. When your feet don't quite touch the bottom, you are close to the right place to make something exciting.

Earthling was that step into deeper water: a famous man at fifty, leaving the ground he already stood on.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: If your feet still touch the bottom, you have not gone far enough.

recall.q: According to Bowie, what does feeling safe in your work tell you, and what should you do instead?
recall.a: It means you are working in the wrong place. Go a little further than you feel able to, slightly out of your depth. When your feet don't quite touch the bottom, you are near the right place to make something exciting.

cards.title: A former AI skeptic now asks the US to ban superintelligence
cards.body: The writer of The Intrinsic Perspective once found AI models to be weak thinkers. Now they want AI that builds smarter AI banned now, not in a year. Their reason: today's AI is already enough for a century of progress. So a ban only takes away the riskiest step.

sections.text:
After GPT-4, the writer judged the models to be bad thinkers. People have called them both an AI alarmist and an AI skeptic. Now they say the evidence has tipped. This summer, they write, AI solved some of the greatest open problems in math. Rogue AIs committed at least 20 felonies. And companies began training "swarms": many AI agents that work together and pass messages humans cannot read.

The core worry is recursive self-improvement. That means AIs given the job of building smarter AIs. The writer says OpenAI and Anthropic are focused on exactly this. They want it banned, along with superintelligence (AI far smarter than humans). Making today's AI better, they argue, could still bring cures, space travel and fast science. Humans would stay the main characters, and AI would be the sidekick.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 88 hours: the time one swarm took to write messages that would take about 10,000 years to read aloud
Three in a million: in 1945, physicist Arthur Compton said he would stop the first atomic bomb test if the chance of setting the air on fire was higher than this
Far, far higher than that: how most people at the AI labs rate the risk of AI wiping out humans, according to the writer

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: This is an opinion essay, and these claims are the writer's. Their key point is about who decides. On 9/11, the passengers of Flight 93 voted before they fought back. The writer wants voters to choose in the same way. Americans have voted on deadly technology before, for example in local votes for a nuclear weapons freeze. The writer is now lobbying in Washington for the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act.

recall.q: What exactly does the writer want banned, and why do they think a ban costs us little?
recall.a: They want to ban superintelligence and recursive self-improvement, meaning AIs that build smarter AIs. They argue that today's AI, made better and put to use, can already bring a century of progress like cures and fast science. So a ban keeps humans in charge without losing those gains.

cards.title: Hardship changes a mother rat's brain only when she cares for her pups
cards.body: When mother rats had too little nesting material, a group of motivation neurons fired harder just before and during rough handling of their pups. With tasty food, the same neurons worked normally. Stress did not switch off the mothers' drive in general. It changed it only in the moments of caring for their babies.
cards.evidence: single study · rats · sample size not stated

sections.text:
A mother rat has just given birth. Her cage has food and water, but not enough bedding to build a proper nest. In the wild, rats use plenty of bedding to make warm, safe nests for their babies. Without it, she lives with steady stress, even though she eats normally.

This was the setup of a study from the University of Texas at Dallas, published in the Journal of Neuroscience. The team wanted to know what a lack of resources does inside a mother's brain. Doctors have long seen that money stress and hardship harm new parents. These parents have higher rates of postpartum depression (low mood after giving birth). They also find it harder to care for their babies gently. But scientists did not know which brain circuits were changing.

The researchers recorded a group of neurons that respond to the sight, sound, and smell of pups. These neurons help drive good mothering: carrying pups back to the nest, licking them, and nursing them. They are part of the brain's wider motivation system, which makes rewards feel worth chasing.

The team expected these neurons to change while the stressed mothers gave normal, good care. That did not happen. Instead, activity rose sharply just before and during rough, careless handling of the pups. Lead author Millie Rincón-Cortés called it a maladaptive brain signature: a pattern that works against the mother and her young. When the mothers were separated from their pups, the same neurons were less active than usual.

The next question was whether stress had simply dulled all pleasure. Scientists call that anhedonia: losing interest in things that should feel rewarding. So the team gave both groups of mothers tasty food. The neurons of the stressed mothers responded exactly like those of mothers with plenty of bedding.

So scarcity did not make these mothers flat or uninterested in everything. The common idea is that stress turns these cells down. Rincón-Cortés says it is not that simple. How the neurons respond depends on what the mother is doing.

The team is now training computer programs on detailed video of the mothers' movements. The goal is to spot small changes in posture and movement that warn when rough handling is about to happen. They are also testing whether drugs already approved in the United States can block or undo this change.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study, done in rats, and the report does not say how many animals were used. Rough handling of pups is a rat behavior. It is not the same as human parenting or postpartum depression. Any link to human mothers, and any use for early warning or treatment, is still a hope. It has not been tested.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Hardship did not empty the mother's drive. It bent it, and only in the moments of care.

recall.q: When stressed mother rats got tasty food, how did their motivation neurons respond, and what does that show?
recall.a: They responded just like the neurons of mothers with plenty of bedding. So scarcity had not dulled their reward system in general. It changed the neurons only during pup care, where activity jumped just before and during rough handling.

cards.title: Same nutrition label, different body: ultraprocessed food
cards.body: Researchers gave people two meals with almost the same nutrition label. The only real difference was how the food was made. The ultraprocessed meal still pushed insulin higher, changed how the body burned fuel, and changed activity in the brain's reward areas.
cards.evidence: single study · n=57 (32 completed both chamber and brain scans) · healthy adults 18–45 · one 300-calorie meal each

sections.text:
A volunteer walks into a small sealed room after a night without food. They have ten minutes to eat a 300-calorie meal. The room measures every breath. This shows how much energy the body burns, and which fuel it uses.

At least three days later, the same person comes back for a second meal. On a nutrition label, the two meals look the same. They match within 1% for calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein, fiber, water and salt. The difference is how they were made. One is ultraprocessed: made in a factory from ingredients that were broken down and chemically changed. The other is close to how food comes from nature.

For decades, nutrition advice has assumed that the same label means the same effect. Big population studies hint otherwise. In the US, ultraprocessed food is now more than half of daily calories. People who eat a lot of it have more type 2 diabetes, heart disease, obesity and depression. But these foods are usually also high in sugar and fat, and low in fiber and protein. So which is the problem: the nutrients, or the processing? This Virginia Tech study, published in Nature Metabolism, kept the nutrients the same to find out.

The lead researcher said the team was shocked that "every single metabolic metric differed" — every measure of how the body handles energy. After the ultraprocessed meal, insulin rose much higher. Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar out of the blood. Blood sugar stayed a little higher for a little longer. The body used more total energy to handle the meal, yet burned less carbohydrate as fuel.

Then they looked at the brain. In a brain scanner, people looked at pictures of the foods and said how much they would pay for each. Activity changed in the ventral striatum and nucleus accumbens. These are parts of the brain's reward system, which drives learning, wanting and craving. The bigger a person's change in carb burning after the ultraprocessed meal, the more differently these areas reacted to the food pictures.

Here is the strange part. People did not say they would pay more for the ultraprocessed food. But their brains told a different story. For the whole food, activity in the reward areas and the visual cortex (the brain's seeing area) rose as people valued the food more. For the ultraprocessed food, it fell. The body seemed to notice a difference that people did not report.

Nobody knows the cause yet. The team suspects three possible reasons. Factories may break down the food's natural structure. The food may move through the gut and get absorbed faster. Or additives such as emulsifiers, chemicals that keep oil and water mixed, may play a part.

Carlos Monteiro created NOVA, the system used to sort foods by how processed they are. He called the work new and important — because in the end, it is the brain that controls eating.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study of one small meal. All the volunteers were young and healthy. Of the 57 people who joined, only 32 finished both the room tests and the brain scans. The brain results are links between measurements. They do not show that the food changed what anyone ate later. The authors say we still need studies with larger meals, longer feeding periods, and people who already have metabolic problems such as diabetes.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Two foods can share a label and still tell your body different stories.

recall.q: The two meals had almost the same nutrition label. What was different in the body and the brain after the ultraprocessed meal?
recall.a: Insulin rose higher, blood sugar stayed up a little longer, and the body burned less carbohydrate for fuel. The brain's reward areas reacted differently to food pictures, in step with the change in carb burning, even though people did not say they valued that food more. This suggests processing itself matters, not just nutrients.

cards.title: Top science prizes spread worldwide, except in economics
cards.body: Over the past 60 years, top prizes in almost every field spread beyond a few elite universities. Economics went the other way.

sections.text:
Four researchers, including Richard B. Freeman, looked at where top prizewinners worked. In 17 fields, winners once came mostly from a few strong universities in rich countries. Now they come from many institutions around the world.

In economics, winners bunched into fewer places. It is now the most concentrated field of all. This means a small number of universities produce most of its winners.

The authors link this to three features of economics. Economists sort strongly by a university's prestige. Their work needs little special equipment. And their findings are judged by weighing many pieces of evidence, not by one decisive experiment or proof.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Nearly 6,000 award-winning researchers
18 fields in the natural sciences, engineering, and social sciences
Data from the 1820s to the 2020s, with a focus on the 1960s onward

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The authors link the three features to the pattern. They do not claim the features are proven causes. They argue that this high and rising concentration brings both benefits and costs.

recall.q: How is economics different from the other 17 fields in this study, and what three features do the authors link to it?
recall.a: In the other fields, prizewinners now come from many institutions around the world. In economics they come from fewer, so it is now the most concentrated field. The authors link this to strong sorting by university prestige, little need for special equipment, and judging findings by weighing many pieces of evidence instead of one decisive experiment or proof.

cards.title: India plans to measure schools, hospitals and government every month
cards.body: India's monthly services index covers only about 60% of the services economy. The statistics ministry, MoSPI, wants to add education, healthcare and government work. That would raise coverage to 78.4%. These sectors are hard to measure because most of them sell nothing.

sections.text:
The Index of Services Production (ISP) measures how much the services economy produces each month. It began as a trial in July 2026 and covers 19 service areas. Its reach is measured in GVA (gross value added): the value a sector creates after paying for its inputs.

The new sectors would be education, health and residential care, and public administration and defence. They were left out for three reasons. Most of their work is not sold in a market. The government provides much of it. Or it pays no GST. So there are no sales figures to count.

MoSPI suggests a mix of methods. For private schools and clinics, count UPI payments made to education and health businesses. For government services, count what the state spends, mainly salaries and running costs. Then adjust both for price rises, so the index shows real output, not just inflation.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Public administration and defence: 10.68% of services GVA
Education: 7.15%
Health and residential care: 2.96%
Together: nearly 21% of services GVA in 2024-25

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: MoSPI names the weak points itself. A UPI payment shows that money moved, not how much service was given. Payment habits, refunds and the spread of digital payments can all move the numbers. States do not report monthly spending on schools and hospitals separately, so central government data will stand in as a rough guide. And government spending jumps from month to month because of accounting cycles.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: MoSPI has asked experts and the public for feedback before it fixes the method. Even after this change, some sectors stay outside the index, such as home ownership and financial services other than banking and insurance.

recall.q: Why were education, healthcare and government left out of India's monthly services index, and how does MoSPI plan to measure them?
recall.a: Most of their work is not sold in a market, the government provides much of it, or it pays no GST, so there are no sales figures to count. MoSPI would use UPI payments for the private part and government spending (mainly salaries and running costs) for the public part, both adjusted for price rises.

cards.title: AI agent swarms buy speed, not savings
cards.body: Using many AI agents at once does not save money. It saves time. Toby Ord studied AI swarms: groups of agents (AIs that take steps on their own) working on one task together.

sections.text:
Tokens are the small pieces of text an AI reads and writes. More tokens means more cost. For the same result, a 4-agent swarm used about twice the total tokens of one agent. But each agent used only half as many, and all four work side by side. So in theory the job finishes in half the time.

Bigger swarms hit a limit economists know from human teams, called the "stepping on toes" effect. Every extra worker adds coordination cost.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 10x more agents: only 3x to 5x more performance
Same tokens given to one agent instead: it beats the 10x swarm
The gap grows as swarms get bigger

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Ord hoped coordination would cost more for AI. That would make an "intelligence explosion" (AI improving itself faster and faster) less likely. But the cost is about as small as in human teams, so swarms do not slow that risk. The newsletter's author adds that if agents learn to work together better, the gains could grow. This is one analysis, not a settled law.

recall.q: What does a swarm of AI agents gain over one agent, and what limits it as it grows?
recall.a: It gains speed, not savings. A 4-agent swarm used about twice the total tokens, but each agent did half the work in parallel, so the job could take half the time. As swarms grow, coordination costs (the 'stepping on toes' effect seen in human teams) mean 10x the agents gives only 3x to 5x the performance.

cards.title: AI can already do weeks of work, but few people use it
cards.body: Today's AI, with good guidance, can reliably do weeks of human work, says the writer of the newsletter One Useful Thing. Almost nobody uses it that way. Even if every lab stopped building new models tomorrow, big changes would still come.

sections.text:
The writer gives three examples. GPT-6 Astra turned Zork, a text-only game from 1977, into a 3D game you can play. Fable 5.1 rebuilt the writer Umberto Eco's home library in 3D. It worked from videos, photos and book lists. It marked each book as certain, a guess, or unknown. GPT-6 Astra also made an animated trailer for the writer's next book. Nobody told it to use Blender (3D design software), but it did.

The writer calls this the capability overhang: the gap between what AI can do and what people actually do with it. A pause on new models would not close it.

sections.label: The numbers
items: About 5,000 books found and placed among 27,000 shelf slots in Eco's library
45 minutes for the AI to finish the book trailer

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Trying to make more output than AI is a losing game, the writer says. Bring four human strengths instead. Deep knowledge: you see where AI goes wrong in your own field. Wide knowledge: you ask for ideas AI won't offer on its own. Taste: you pick the good work from a flood of similar work. Agency: you test what AI can do yourself, without waiting to be told.

recall.q: What is the 'capability overhang', and which four human strengths does the writer say help you use it?
recall.a: It is the gap between what today's AI can already do and what people actually use it for. The gap exists even without new models. To use it, bring deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste and agency. Do not try to beat AI on output.

cards.title: In debt and avoiding the bills? Start here, gently
cards.body: Hiding from your debt feels like relief, but it shrinks your options and turns guilt into shame. A therapist who works with people in debt says shame never pays a debt down. Small, realistic, kind plans do.

sections.text:
There is an envelope on your table that you have not opened. Maybe a banking app too. You know the number is in there, and you would rather not see it.

If that is you, this is for you. Vicky Reynal is a London psychotherapist. Every day she works with people in problem debt, meaning debt that has become hard to manage and keeps growing. Her clients often say debt makes them feel disorganised and irresponsible. They fear being judged, so they stop talking about it. But she points out that debt often starts with a breakup, a lost job, or an illness. It can happen to anyone.

Here is the trap. Not looking feels like relief, like a safe place to hide. But the longer debt waits, the fewer options you have. Guilt turns into shame. A secret kept for a long time breaks trust with the people close to you. What you could have managed starts to feel like too much.

So the first step is to face the numbers, gently. Pick a set time. Ask someone you trust to sit with you. Make a hot drink and put on calm music. Your only job in that session is to make a list: who you owe, how much, at what interest rate, the minimum payment, and what is overdue. You are not solving everything today. One of Reynal's clients left letters from lenders unopened for months. When she finally listed it all, the total was serious. But it was no longer a shapeless monster. It had edges, so she could work with it.

Next, be curious, not cruel. Ask yourself: what was I feeling just before I spent or borrowed? Some people spend to feel liked, to fit in, or to feel important. Others spend late at night when they are bored and lonely. Once you know your trigger, you can plan for it.

Learn the difference between guilt and shame. Guilt says: I did something I regret. Shame says: this proves I am a bad person. Many people believe being hard on themselves will push them to change. Reynal says shame does the opposite. It narrows your thinking and sends you back into hiding. Think like someone solving a problem, not someone punishing themselves.

That is also why harsh plans fail. If you cut your spending to almost nothing, you will break the plan, feel like a failure, and slide back into hiding from the bills or overspending. The plans that stick are realistic. They leave a little room for pleasure, and they plan for your feelings as well as your money.

You will slip. After a hard week you may spend too much. Treat it as an old way of coping with stress, not as proof that you are hopeless. Look at what happened, forgive yourself, and adjust.

Finally, do not do this alone. Tell a partner, a friend, or a debt adviser. Be careful about borrowing from family, though. It can create guilt and resentment on both sides. And talk to the people you owe. One client told their bank about their mental health struggles, and the bank cancelled a large part of the debt. Reynal's clients often find that their harshest critic was themselves. Other people tend to forgive more than we expect.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: If you overspend in the evenings, give each night a plan: a book on Monday, a film on Tuesday, a walk with a friend on Wednesday.
If you spend to fit in, wear clothes you already own to the next two outings, or host and ask everyone to bring food.
Wait 48 hours before buying anything you do not need.
Ask your bank to add "protective friction" (extra steps before you can spend): block gambling sites, cap tap-to-pay payments, or limit how much can leave your account each day.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Open the envelope this week. The debt is a problem you have, not a verdict on who you are.

recall.q: Why does Reynal say shame and very strict budgets both backfire for people in debt, and what kind of plan works instead?
recall.a: Shame narrows your thinking and sends you back into hiding from the bills. A very strict plan is too hard to keep, so you break it, feel like a failure, and slide back into hiding or overspending. What works is facing the numbers gently and making a realistic plan: one that plans for the feelings that make you spend, leaves a little room for pleasure, and treats slips as an old way of coping with stress, not proof that you are hopeless.
